newsitem.title: USA: U.S. soybean, corn acres this year highest since 80s.
newsitem.headline: U.S. soybean, corn acres this year highest since 80s.

text.p: Responding to the highest soybean prices in almost nine years and the least government involvement in more than 60, U.S. farmers plan to plant 68.8 million acres of soybeans this year -- the most since 1980, the government said Monday.

The Agriculture Department, making its first report on what American farmers will plant this spring, said a national survey of 55,000 producers showed farmers will also plant 81.4 million acres of corn, the largest corn acreage in 12 years, as they take advantage of the new-found planting flexibility provided by last year's overhaul of U.S. farm policy.

The government estimates were sharply above expectations of commodity traders and analysts, and corn and soybean prices at the Chicago Board of Trade fell in response to the report and in anticipation of big crops this year.
"The acreage numbers are humongous," Steve Bruce of the E.D. and F. Man International commodity brokerage said in a telephone interview.
Soybeans for delivery in November, after the new crop is harvested, closed at $6.93 a bushel, down 21 cents, and corn for December delivery closed at $2.91-1/2, down 5 cents.
Corn and soybeans are the nation's biggest money-making crops. Last year's U.S. corn crop was valued at almost $25 billion, while soybean production was worth more than $16 billion.
Big plantings this spring of the two crops sets the stage for near-record harvests.

Assuming good weather and average yields, U.S. soybean production this year could total more than 2.5 billion bushels, close to 1994's record of 2.52 billion. The corn harvest could reach more than 9.6 billion bushels, compared with the record crop in 1994 of 10.1 billion.

The government's closely watched estimates -- released in the Agriculture Department's annual Prospective Plantings report -- also projected U.S. wheat plantings to be down across the board as farmers chose to plant the more profitable soybeans and corn.

Spring wheat and durum wheat plantings showed the biggest decreases at 17.8 million and 3.19 million acres respectively. Total U.S. wheat acreage this year is estimated at 69.2 million acres, down almost 10 percent from last year.
Cotton acreage was anticipated to be down slightly at 14.5 million acres, with acreage down in California due to flooding and down in the Delta states as farmers shift to soybeans.

Taken together, corn and soybean plantings of 150.2 million acres are similar to conditions in the late 1970s and early 1980s, said Ray Halley, chief of the crops branch of the Agriculture Department's National Agriculture Statistics Service, which calculated the estimates.

Halley said the upturn in corn and soybean plantings comes largely at the expense of wheat and sorghum, especially in "fringe" areas like North Dakota which saw the biggest jump in bean acreage -- up 250,000 acres -- of any single state.

Twenty-six of the 29 soybean-growing states in the nation reported plans to increase bean plantings. Increases in the Southeast, where corn and soybeans are often rotated or soybeans are planted after wheat, were especially big. The Agriculture Department said bean acreage is "expected to increase significantly across all of the Southeastern states."

Soybeans have shown a tremendous growth in the United States since the early 1960s, with production quadrupling. Limited foreign competition, along with soaring demand for soy products, have sparked U.S. plantings.

This year's planting decisions stem from the so-called "Freedom to Farm" legislation signed into law last April. The new farm policy swept aside a system in place since the New Deal and removed most federal control over farmers, allowing them to move from crop to crop in pursuit of profits.
